Laboratory-reared cohorts of the mysterious bobtail squid, Sepietta obscura, maintained at a constant water temperature of 16.5 °C [T = 16.5 °C], provided detailed life-history data. Hatchlings emerged from their fertilised ova after an embryonic incubation period of 45 days [ab = 45 days] at a temperature of 16.5 °C [T = 16.5 °C]. At the moment of yolk-sac resorption and the onset of exogenous feeding, these neonates possessed a minute mantle length of just 0.2 cm [Lb = 0.2 cm] and a correspondingly low wet weight of 0.004 grams [Wwb = 0.004 grams]. This initial body mass, derived from allometric scaling relationships observed in other sepiolids such as Sepiola atlantica, underscores the substantial energetic investment required during early planktonic life.

Field surveys and captive growth studies indicate that Sepietta obscura experiences a notably compressed developmental schedule under thermal conditions typical of its Mediterranean habitat. The transition through the juvenile phase culminates in the attainment of sexual maturity, marked by the onset of gametogenesis, which occurs when individuals reach a mantle length of 1.6 cm [Lp = 1.6 cm]. At this pubertal threshold, the corresponding wet weight of the animals is approximately 2.1 grams [Wwp = approximately 2.1 grams]. This size at maturation is reached relatively quickly; calculations based on individual growth trajectories at 16.5 °C [T = 16.5 °C] demonstrate that the time since birth at puberty is 115 days since birth [tp = 115 days since birth], a rapid pace that aligns with the species’ short semelparous life cycle.

Adults of Sepietta obscura achieve their maximum somatic dimensions following the completion of exponential growth. The ultimate mantle length recorded for fully grown, reproductively active individuals is 2.4 cm [Li = 2.4 cm]. This final mantle size corresponds to a maximum live wet weight of 6.9 grams [Wwi = 6.9 grams], reflecting a substantial increase from the pubertal mass as energy is directed toward tissue upkeep and the development of reproductive tissues. Consistently, the overall lifespan of this species is tightly constrained; the oldest documented individuals, monitored under controlled laboratory conditions at the same temperature regime, survived for a maximum of 230 days [am = 230 days] at 16.5 °C [T = 16.5 °C]. This abbreviated lifespan is characteristic of small, fast-living coastal cephalopods.

Reproductive output in Sepietta obscura is concentrated into a single, terminal spawning event, following which the gravid individuals undergo senescence and eventual biological death. Under stable thermal conditions of 16.5 °C [T = 16.5 °C], the cumulative reproductive output at death was recorded as 125 eggs . This total fecundity appears modest relative to larger pelagic squids but is consistent with the limited body cavity and short reproductive window of this diminutive benthic species. Histological examination of the gonads from post-pubertal adults confirms that oocyte development proceeds simultaneously, with all eggs being ovulated in a single batch before physiological deterioration sets in. There is no evidence of multiple spawning cycles.

A comparative perspective reveals that the growth and reproductive metrics of Sepietta obscura align closely with those of its congeners. For instance, the maximum recorded longevity of approximately 230 days [am = approximately 230 days] is typical for small sepiolids adapted to warm, at a temperature of 16.5 °C [T = 16.5 °C]shallow waters. Similarly, the observed hatchling size of 0.2 cm [Lb = 0.2 cm] mantle length places this species among the smallest neonates in the family Sepiolidae, a trait that may influence its early mortality risk and dispersal potential. The adult wet weight of 6.9 grams [Wwi = 6.9 grams] represents a roughly seventeen-hundred-fold increase relative to the initial 0.004 grams [Wwb = 0.004 grams], a growth factorial that underscores the rapid biomass accumulation permitted by a high metabolic rate in these temperate waters. These data provide a robust baseline for future physiological studies.
